details:
**"The Second Coming" and the "rough beast"**
Yeats's most famous poem (1919), an apocalyptic vision written in the aftermath of World War I. It ends by asking "what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?" The speaker sees "a vast image out of Spiritus Mundi," the world's collective soul: a sphinx-like shape "with lion body and the head of a man," whose "twenty centuries of stony sleep / Were vexed to nightmare by a rocking cradle."

**"Turning and turning in the widening gyre"**
The opening of "The Second Coming," which continues "The falcon cannot hear the falconer; / Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; / Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world." It goes on to say "the ceremony of innocence is drowned" and "The best lack all conviction, while the worst / Are full of passionate intensity." The gyre, a widening spiral, reflects Yeats's cyclical theory of history, which he set out in A Vision.

**"Sailing to Byzantium" and "That is no country for old men"**
A poem from The Tower (1928) in which an aging speaker leaves the sensual world of the young and sails to the holy city of Byzantium. Its first line, "That is no country for old men," supplied the title of Cormac McCarthy's novel No Country for Old Men. The speaker says there is no "singing school but studying / Monuments of its own magnificence."

**"An aged man is but a paltry thing"**
A line from "Sailing to Byzantium," which continues "A tattered coat upon a stick, unless / Soul clap its hands and sing." The speaker asks the "sages standing in God's holy fire / As in the gold mosaic of a wall" to free his heart, "sick with desire / And fastened to a dying animal," and "gather me / Into the artifice of eternity." Once "out of nature," he wants to take "such a form as Grecian goldsmiths make," a golden bird singing to a drowsy emperor.

**"Easter, 1916" and "A terrible beauty is born"**
Yeats's poem on the failed Easter Rising against British rule in Dublin, whose leaders were executed. He recalls passing them with "polite meaningless words" and mocking them "to please a companion / Around the fire at the club," but now "All changed, changed utterly: / A terrible beauty is born." He also warns that "Too long a sacrifice / Can make a stone of the heart."

**"MacDonagh and MacBride / And Connolly and Pearse"**
The executed Easter Rising leaders whom Yeats names at the end of "Easter, 1916," saying "I write it out in a verse" for "wherever green is worn." John MacBride, the estranged husband of Yeats's beloved Maud Gonne, is the "drunken, vainglorious lout" who "had done most bitter wrong" but is still honored.

**"The Lake Isle of Innisfree"**
An early lyric (1890) about an island in Lough Gill, County Sligo, where Yeats spent much of his childhood. It begins "I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree, / And a small cabin build there, of clay and wattles made." The speaker will have "nine bean-rows" and "live alone in the bee-loud glade," where "peace comes dropping slow," "midnight's all a glimmer," and evening is "full of the linnet's wings."

**"Leda and the Swan"**
A 1923 sonnet about Zeus, in the form of a swan, raping the Spartan queen Leda, which leads to the birth of Helen and the Trojan War. It opens "A sudden blow: the great wings beating still," and the act "engenders there / The broken wall, the burning roof and tower / And Agamemnon dead." It ends by asking "Did she put on his knowledge with his power / Before the indifferent beak could let her drop?"

**"The Circus Animals' Desertion" and "the foul rag and bone shop of the heart"**
A late poem (1939) in which the aging poet "sought a theme and sought for it in vain" and asks "What can I but enumerate old themes?" Reviewing his past work, he finds it rose from "old iron, old bones, old rags." He concludes that now his ladder is gone, "I must lie down where all the ladders start, / In the foul rag and bone shop of the heart."

**"The Wild Swans at Coole"**
A poem set at Coole Park, the estate of Yeats's patron Lady Gregory. It begins "The nineteenth autumn has come upon me / Since I first made my count" of the "nine-and-fifty swans," which "scatter wheeling in great broken rings / Upon their clamorous wings." Unlike the aging poet, the swans paddle "lover by lover" in the "cold / Companionable streams," and "their hearts have not grown old."

**"Among School Children"**
A poem from The Tower in which Yeats, as "a sixty-year-old smiling public man" and senator, visits a convent school. It ends "O body swayed to music, O brightening glance, / How can we know the dancer from the dance?"

**"An Irish Airman Foresees His Death"**
A poem spoken by Major Robert Gregory, Lady Gregory's son, who was killed flying in World War I. He says "I know that I shall meet my fate / Somewhere among the clouds above; / Those that I fight I do not hate, / Those that I guard I do not love," and that he fights out of "a lonely impulse of delight." Yeats also mourned him in "In Memory of Major Robert Gregory."

**Things Fall Apart**
Chinua Achebe took the title of his 1958 novel from "The Second Coming." In it, Okonkwo is exiled to his mother's village after his gun accidentally kills a 16-year-old boy, and his uncle Uchendu teaches him that "Mother is Supreme."

**W. H. Auden's "In Memory of W. B. Yeats"**
Auden's 1939 elegy for Yeats, who died that January. It begins "He disappeared in the dead of winter: / The brooks were frozen, the airports almost deserted," declares "mad Ireland hurt you into poetry" and "poetry makes nothing happen," and includes the lines "Earth, receive an honoured guest: / William Yeats is laid to rest."

**"Tread softly because you tread on my dreams"**
The closing line of "He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven," often linked to Yeats's unrequited love for Maud Gonne. The poor speaker wishes he had "the heavens' embroidered cloths" to spread under the beloved's feet, but has only his dreams to offer.
